h1: Regulatory affairs jobs at beer companies
title: Regulatory Affairs Jobs in Brewing | Craft Beer School
desc: What regulatory affairs staff do at beer companies in India, the skills the role needs, how people get in from law, food science or brewing and where it leads.
teaser: In India a beer cannot move from a tank to a shelf without a paper trail. Regulatory affairs is the team that keeps it moving.
standfirst: Alcohol is regulated state by state in India. Every new beer, label and pack goes through some kind of approval. That makes regulatory affairs one of the quieter but steadier careers around a brewery.
sections:
Regulatory affairs sits between the brewery and the authorities. The team makes sure the company holds the licences it needs, that every product and label meets the rules and that returns and payments are filed on time. When something changes in a notification, they are the first to read it and tell the others.

It is a desk and phone job with regular site visits. You are likely to spend more time with documents, officers and brand and operations colleagues than with brewing vessels. But you need to understand the vessels well enough to know what the paperwork describes.
Why India makes it a job of its own

Alcohol is a state subject, so licensing, brand registration, label rules, duty and movement permits are handled state by state. A national brewery therefore works with many sets of rules at once. They also change. A small brewery may handle one state with one adviser. A larger company keeps a team.

Beyond state excise, other rules touch a beer. Food safety regulation covers standards and labelling for alcoholic beverages. Packaged goods rules cover declarations on the pack. Environmental and factory approvals apply to the plant. Rules and their names change, so a person in this job spends a lot of time checking what applies now. We do not give legal advice here. We describe the shape of the work.

The week is rarely dull because it follows other people's deadlines. It might include:

  • Preparing a label for approval in a new state and checking each claim and warning against the current rules.
  • Tracking licence renewals so none lapses.
  • Filing production and stock returns to the excise department.
  • Answering an officer's query about a batch or a pack.
  • Briefing marketing on what a label or an offer can and cannot say.

The pressure peaks at launches and before festival seasons, when several approvals have to land in the same weeks. Good teams keep a tracker of every application, with its date, its officer and its next step.

Brand teams respect the person who tells them early that a design needs a change. They do not respect the one who tells them after printing.

Patience and accuracy come first. A wrong date or a missing document can hold up a launch for weeks. Next comes writing, because you will draft applications and replies that an officer must understand on one read. Then comes relationship building. People who work well with excise and food officers, politely and without shortcuts, are valuable.

A working grasp of brewing helps in daily conversations. You should know a strength from a pack size, a production run from a batch and what a label claim means in a tank. Our guide to the jobs inside a brewery shows where the function fits.

There is no single route. Some come from law or company secretarial work. Some come from food science or chemistry and move across from food regulation. Others start in brewery operations or quality and shift into compliance when they enjoy the documents more than the shift. A brewing background is a real advantage, because you can read a technical specification without calling the brewer for every question.

If you are a career changer, learn the process before you apply. A short course such as Brewing Fundamentals teaches the stages a licence or label refers to. Then read the excise rules of one state, closely, to see how the paperwork follows the process.
How it connects to other teams

Regulatory work touches the whole company. Supply chain relies on movement permits, which links to supply chain and procurement jobs in drinks companies. Finance depends on correct duty calculations. Analysts depend on clean returns, which is where data and analytics jobs meet this function. A regulatory person who also understands data is rare and useful.

With experience you can lead a state team, move to a national or regional head role or join an industry body. Some move to consultancies that help new breweries with licences. Others move into quality or operations leadership because they understand how compliance shapes the plant. The role rewards people who stay calm when a notification changes.

Responsible marketing and serving rules also sit here, so people in this job tend to care about how alcohol is sold. That is a good trait in a company that wants to last.
faqs: What does a regulatory affairs person do at a beer company?
They manage licences, label and brand approvals, excise returns and changes in rules. They also advise brand and operations teams on what is allowed.
Do I need a law degree for regulatory affairs?
No. People come from law, food science, chemistry, operations and quality. What matters is accuracy, patience and a good grasp of the process.
Are alcohol rules the same across India?
No. Alcohol is a state subject, so licences, brand registration and label rules differ by state and change. Always check the current notification.
Is a brewing background useful in regulatory work?
Yes. Knowing the process lets you read specifications and describe products correctly on forms.
